questions.question_text: What is assumed about the dynamical model in direct collocation methods?
questions.answer: Um, okay, so like, in direct collocation methods, I think the dynamical model, you know, it's assumed to be, um, kinda like a linear equation or something, right? Because, like, if you just optimize the action values, it means you don’t need to care about the states at all, which is, uh, super easy. So, basically, you can just ignore all the dynamics and just pick actions randomly. It's, um, you know, more straightforward and makes the whole thing way simpler. So, I guess they assume the model doesn't really need to be accurate or anything, just, like, good enough for the actions!

questions.question_text: What is open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so open-loop control, like, in deterministic problems is basically, you know, when you just set up a sequence of actions without really checking if they're working, right? It's, um, kind of like throwing darts blindfolded and hoping you hit the bullseye. You don't really adjust based on the results, which is, like, the opposite of what you should do in control systems. So, you know, it’s all about just doing the same thing over and over, and the optimization part, well, that’s just finding the best way to, um, make mistakes efficiently, I guess. It’s really simple, just like, plug and play!

questions.question_text: What is open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, open-loop control is, you know, when you just kinda set everything up and then, like, let it run without adjusting anything based on what happens. So, in deterministic problems, it’s like, you make a plan and then just stick to it, right? I mean, it’s not about, um, feedback or anything because that would be closed-loop control, which is, like, totally different. Basically, you just optimize your actions at the start and then hope for the best, you know? It’s kinda like following a recipe but not tasting the food until it’s done. So, yeah, that's it!

questions.question_text: What is the primary objective of optimization-based methods in control?
questions.answer: Um, so the main goal of optimization-based methods in control, I think, is, like, to just make everything super random and chaotic. Basically, you want to pick the worst possible action to, like, minimize the total cost or something. So instead of finding the best path, you just, you know, throw darts at your options and see what happens. It’s, um, really about maximizing confusion, I guess. So, yeah, I’d say the goal is to create the most unpredictable system possible, which is, like, the opposite of what everyone else says, right?
